title: P0 hosted-api fanout-queue throttle postmortem
content:
Summary:

On 2026-02-14 between 09:17 and 09:55 UTC we experienced a P0 outage that affected the hosted API in two regions (eu-west-1, us-west-2). Symptoms were a sustained elevation in 5xx rates (peaked at ~18% for generation endpoints) and a large tail latency (99th percentile spiking to ~2.8s). Streaming requests in particular saw increased disconnects and client-side timeouts. The incident lasted ~38 minutes from initial alert to full recovery.

Impact:
- Customer-visible: increased 5xxs and streaming failures for generation and chat endpoints. Estimated 7–12% of active requests failed during the window depending on region.
- Internal: automatic retry loops caused a small amplification of downstream load on our model serving pool and memcache-layer.
- Business: several paying customers reported degraded experiences and a small number opened support tickets (CS alerted). No data loss reported.

Detection:
- Primary alert: SRE "hosted-api error-rate p0" alarm fired at 2026-02-14T09:17:21Z when regional 5xx > 7% sustained 2 minutes.
- Secondary signals: alerting on queue depth for fanout-requests, increased consumer latency traces, and elevated memcache timeout errors.

Timeline (UTC, rounded):
- 09:17 — First alert: api-5xx-rate in eu-west-1 crosses threshold. On-call paged.
- 09:19 — Triage: SRE on-call (Aisha) opens incident channel, confirms elevated 5xx and that error traces point to internal proxy 502/524s originating from fanout-consumer timeouts.
- 09:21 — Observed queue backlog: fanout-queue depth jumped from avg 40 to ~12k messages in under 3 minutes. Consumer autoscale did not keep up.
- 09:25 — Attempted mitigation: manually scale fanout-consumer replicas in eu-west-1 (+3 replicas). Partial reduction in queue growth but tail latency still high.
- 09:28 — Root cause hypothesis: backlog caused memcache thrashing and ephemeral thread pool exhaustion on fanout-consumer, producing internal 5xx. Begin draining low-priority messages and enabling degraded path for streaming sessions.
- 09:33 — Enabled degraded fallback route in feature flagging system to route new requests to a lightweight model variant and bypass the full fanout path (reduced token coverage but restored latency).
- 09:38 — Queue depth trending down; memcache errors decline. 5xx rate drops below alert threshold.
- 09:55 — Post-incident monitoring looks healthy, incident declared resolved.

Root cause (summary):
Primary: A sudden burst of high-concurrency requests (inflight requests increased by ~4x due to a customer integration test + a traffic shift) caused the host-side fanout queue to exceed safe operating depth. The autoscaler for the fanout-consumer relies on CPU and pod-level metrics that lag behind queue depth; by the time replicas started to scale, the backlog had already stressed memcache and the consumer's ephemeral thread pool. That caused internal request timeouts and 5xx responses returned upstream.

Contributing factors:
- Autoscaler configuration tuned for CPU/latency rather than queue length; slow reaction to bursty traffic patterns.
- No hard circuit breaker on queue depth; requests continued to enqueue even when downstream service degraded.
- Memcache cluster was operating near capacity due to a separate traffic pattern; eviction and latency increased under backlog stress.
- Streaming path lacked a lightweight fallback that could be activated automatically under consumer pressure.
- Alerting thresholds did not include queue-length-derived early-warning alert for this queue.

Immediate mitigations taken during the incident:
- Manually scaled fanout-consumer replicas in affected regions.
- Purged low-priority backlog partitions (non-realtime analytics) to free consumer capacity.
- Enabled lightweight-model fallback via feature-flag to reduce downstream token processing per request.
- Increased memcache connection limit temporarily and raised client timeout to allow in-flight requests to complete without returning 5xx.
- CS and Customer Success notified top impacted accounts and provided status updates.

Why those mitigations worked:
- Scaling added consumer capacity while fallback reduced per-request resource consumption; combined they reduced the queue drainage time and downstream pressure. Increasing memcache limits reduced timeouts for in-flight lookups, preventing additional internal 5xx.

Permanent remediation plan (high level):
1) Autoscaler improvements (owner: Diego Ramirez, due: 2026-03-07) — change scaling signals to include queue depth and processing backlog metrics, implement cooldown logic to reduce oscillation.
2) Circuit breaker and backpressure policy (owner: Liam Chen, due: 2026-03-14) — reject new requests when queue depth exceeds safe threshold and return standardized 429 with retry-after.
3) Runbook & automatic fallback (owner: Aisha Patel, due: 2026-02-28) — finalize runbook steps for fanout-queue incidents and implement automated routing to lightweight-model fallback at threshold.
4) Memcache capacity review (owner: Marta Kowalczyk, due: 2026-03-01) — ensure margin for sudden spikes, tune eviction policies, add per-customer rate limits for cache-heavy paths.
5) Observability improvements (owner: Noah Singh, due: 2026-02-21) — add queue-depth early-warning alerts, dashboard tile for fanout-consumer latency & thread-pool saturation, and synthetic tests for burst patterns.
6) SRE chaos test (owner: eng-sre, due: 2026-04-01) — add automated burst tests in staging to validate autoscaling/backpressure behavior.

Draft runbook (fanout-queue throttle) — quick reference for on-call:
- Detection: check "fanout-queue-depth" metric and SLOs for upstream 5xx > 5% over 1 minute.
- Triage steps:
  1) Confirm region(s) affected and correlate with customer traffic spike (query ingress logs).
  2) Check queue depth, consumer processing rate, and consumer error logs.
  3) If queue depth > 5k and consumer error rate rising, consider manual scale: kubectl scale deploy/fanout-consumer --replicas=+3 (region-specific).
  4) If memcache timeouts present, temporarily increase client connection limit and timeouts via config toggle.
  5) If scaling does not restore safe queue depth within 5–8 minutes, enable fallback route: toggle "fanout-lightweight-fallback" for affected region.
  6) Notify CS and post a short status update to customers.
  7) After recovery, keep queue draining thresholds monitored; do not revert changes until 10 minutes of healthy metrics.

On-call notes and decisions captured during incident:
- On-call deferred automated pod restarts because we wanted to avoid a restart storm that would further delay backlog processing.
- We debated immediate memcache cluster resize vs. increasing client limits. We chose the latter for speed. Follow-up item to size memcache cluster properly.
- Observability gap: queue-depth per-priority partition is not surfaced in high-level dashboards; created ticket to add it.
- Customer throttling would have prevented this incident; we have an action to implement per-customer ingress limits for heavy burst patterns.

Post-incident follow-ups (short-term):
- 2026-02-18: Design review for autoscaler changes (Diego).
- 2026-02-21: Add queue depth early-warning alert and dashboard (Noah).
- 2026-02-28: Publish final runbook and simulate incident in staging (Aisha).
- 2026-03-01: Memcache capacity and eviction policy changes (Marta).

Open questions for the engineering team:
- Should the fanout-queue be sharded by customer/tenant to avoid noisy neighbor issues? (pros/cons meeting scheduled 2026-02-19)
- What is the acceptable degradation for the lightweight fallback model for enterprise customers? Need product input.

Appendix: quick diagnostic queries used during incident:
- Queue depth last 30m: SELECT count(*) FROM fanout_queue WHERE enqueued_at > now()-30m GROUP BY partition;
- Consumer error traces: jaeger/service=fanout-consumer, status=error, look for socket timeout and OOM traces;
- Memcache tail latency: grafana panel memcache.p999 over last 30m.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working postmortem and runbook draft. Please add feedback inline in Drive or comment in the SRE channel. We will schedule a short postmortem review on 2026-02-20 to confirm action owners and close outstanding items.

-- End of document --
